newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic sacrifices growth for social peace.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic sacrifices growth for social peace.

text.p: The year which Serbia's ruling Socialists promised to be one of reforms, growth and stability is turning into a political nightmare of strikes and increasing poverty as elections approach.

President Slobodan Milosevic is facing a stark dilemma -- to tightly control monetary policy or come to grips with an expected burst of social tension ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections by the end of the year, analysts say.

The state wants to avoid printing money but it is hard pressed to come up with the cash to stop the increasing delays in payouts to pensioners, doctors and nurses, teachers and disenchanted workers in the country.

"Milosevic's government is in a tight spot with no prospect in sight of the country's return to the world financial organisations and not one single growth generator at home," said Dana Popovic, of private centre for economic studies CES-Mecon.

"If money is to be released in this near-bankrupt economy in no time we would face spiraling inflation again. And that is unacceptable as people still remember 1993, when daily inflation rocketed to 60 percent," she told Reuters.

Another analyst, who asked not to be named, said inflation did not suit "Milosevic's cartel of new entrepreneurs" and that was why it was unlikely he would resort to printing money to placate pensioners and workers, even though they are his bedrock supporters.
The government set a goal of economic stability through price freezes and no changes in the dinar rate this year. It targets a growth of 14 percent.

So far the state has managed through strict monetary policy to stabilise prices and keep inflation at a very low monthly level of 0.1 percent in April, one percent in March, 0.6 in February and 1.4 percent in January.
"Increasing poverty and further drops in standard of living which pushed purchasing power to a minimum level also affected the prices and caused their fall," the expert said.
Experts agreed inflation slow-down was not such a bad thing for the current economic situation but the question was how long the government would be able to keep it under control.

"There is a growing pressure for wages rises from government-controlled big companies which operate at very high costs and incur the biggest losses," Zoran Popov, a Belgrade think-tank Economics Institute analyst, said.
"Monetary policy is just fine tuning the economy. What we need here is a rough tuning -- radical reforms to start with public spending cuts and fiscal policy reform," he said.
"The expected growth is impossible to reach without fresh working capital and structural reforms," he added.
Analysts agreed revoking benefits inherited from the past communist-system would be a political suicide for any party.
"It is a very hot political issue which is unlikely to be resolved in the near future. And Milosevic is too good player to take such a risk," one western diplomat said.

Diplomatic sources see sale of the republic's big monopoly-systems such as Serbia's post and telecommunications company as the only way for Milosevic to overcome financial sanctions and secure fresh foreign funds.
"The situation is obviously alarming and can last only a short time judging by the great haste Milosevic is in to sell the PTT," said another western diplomat.
